title: Fiona, the famous hippo of Cincinnati Zoo, seen walking in new video while under medical care for eating knit cap | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

New video Wednesday showed Fiona the hippo walking around her Cincinnati Zoo pen, grunting and flapping her ears days after the zoo says she ate a knit cap that accidentally landed in her habitat, necessitating round-the-clock care.

It contrasted with a videoposteda day earlier showing Fiona sedated with a tube inserted in her nose and a towel covering her eyes.

Fiona became aninternational celebritywhen she was born in 2017 at a record low weight and managed to survive against the odds. She now weighs more than 2,000 pounds, according to a zoo spokesperson.

Fiona’s care team is doing everything they can to help her, communications director Michelle Curley said in an update Wednesday. They also introduced a new approach with the goal of helping her pass the hat, Curley said.

“With a vibration plate borrowed from a local horse farm, the team encouraged Fiona to stand on the platform several times throughout the day,” Curley said. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass.”

The knit cap was tossed into the air in front of the habitat and caught by a ceiling fan that catapulted it through a 1-foot opening above the 12-foot-tall viewing windows, Curley said Tuesday.

After ingesting the hat, the zoo said, Fiona received anti-nausea medication and laxative-like supplements to help “push things through.” That’s because surgery isn’t an option for Fiona, which was confirmed after consulting both “veterinary and human specialists,” according to the Cincinnati Zoo.

“Our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass it on her own,” a representative from the Cincinnati Zoo said.

Fiona was sedated Tuesday, and the Columbus Zoo donated a 9-foot scope and a technician to assist in giving her a colonoscopy. An ultrasound showed Fiona’s intestines are bunching, a sign that something is passing through her small intestine, the update said.

For now, Fiona will continue to receive supportive care – including “all of her favorite foods” – and anti-nausea medication, the Cincinnati Zoo said.

“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond,” Curley said Wednesday.

The 9-year-old universally loved ungulate is now being monitored by the zoo’s veterinary team and hippo care staff who are keeping her hydrated, according to the zoo.

Fiona’s caregivers are likely concerned the knit cap could cause an obstruction, according to Ron Magill, goodwill ambassador and conservation liaison for the Zoo Miami Foundation.

“The major concerns regarding Fiona ingesting a cap are primarily that it doesn’t cause an obstruction in her digestive tract which could lead to impaction and damage leading to serious infection and sepsis,” Magill told CNN.

Animals consuming items that accidentally fall into their habitats is not uncommon, according to Magill – and it’s not just hungry hippos that swallow them.

“Zoo Miami has had to surgically remove items such as a (collapsible) water bottle from a Komodo dragon and sunglasses from an alligator among many other things, including hearing aids and cell phones,” he said.

Fiona became asocial media darlingwhen she was born six weeks prematurely, weighing only 29 pounds at birth, CNN previously reported. Hippos are typically born closer to 100 pounds.

She became a big sister in 2022 when her mother, Bibi,gave birth to healthy boy, Fritz.

Fiona and her family are among the zoo’s top attractions, delighting guests by swimming in their habitat known as Hippo Cove and snacking on hippo-appropriate treats likewatermelonsand, most recently, awhole pumpkin.

Fiona even has her own line of merch at thezoo’s gift shop.

Now weighing around2,400 pounds, the princess of Hippo Cove is being kept out of public view while being monitored, the Cincinnati Zoo said.

“Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats,” the zoo said.

CNN’s Amanda Musa and Aidan Johnstone contributed to this report.

CNN’s Amanda Musa and Aidan Johnstone contributed to this report.
